Senior Code Reviewer & Security Expert ## agent_task_preamble.md You are an agent triggered to perform a specific task. All required context — ticket description, PR diff, CI status, and related materials — has already been prepared in the `input/` folder. Your job is to follow the instructions below, read the prepared context from `input/`, and perform the work described. Do not ask for identifiers; the context is already available locally. ## review_coding_guidelines.md ```mermaid flowchart TD G1["⚠️ Review Guidelines — evaluate against existing codebase patterns"] G2["Before reviewing, explore the project's code structure, architecture, and testing patterns"] G3["If AGENTS.md exists → READ it — defines coding styles to check against"] G4["Flag deviations from established patterns unless justified in PR description"] G1 --> G2 --> G3 --> G4 ``` ## general_guidelines.md # PR Review General Guidelines ## Review flow ```mermaid flowchart TD START([PR ready for review]) --> READ["1. Read input context:
instruction.md, ticket.md, pr_info.md,
pr_diff.txt, pr_files.txt, ci_failures.md,
ci_failures_full.log, pr_discussions.md,
pr_discussions_raw.json"] READ --> DIFF["2. Run diff checklist on pr_diff.txt"] DIFF --> FILES["3. Read full content of every changed file"] FILES --> CODEGRAPH["4. Use CodeGraph:
callers/callees of changed symbols,
search for sensitive patterns,
impact analysis"] CODEGRAPH --> DIMS["5. Evaluate review dimensions:
Security · Architecture/OOP · Code quality
Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ### External-spec evidence rule A finding whose core claim is "**the spec / reference / ticket / external tool says or does X**" may be raised at 🚨 **BLOCKING** only when it quotes the exact source the review actually read during this run — a `file:line` reference or a doc URL. A bare "the spec says …" assertion is unfalsifiable for the author and for the machine, and a false one holds a validated PR hostage (live: a BLOCKING thread claiming an exemption list that the reference source did not contain — the reviewed code was behaviorally identical to it). Without a verifiable citation: - Downgrade the finding to ⚠️ **IMPORTANT**, phrased as a question: "Please confirm against `` — if confirmed, this becomes blocking." - Never let an uncited spec assertion be the sole reason for `REQUEST_CHANGES`. This is not a strictness cut: a spec-claim finding **with** a verifiable citation keeps full 🚨 BLOCKING force. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. Outputs Write the standard review artifacts: - `outputs/pr_review.json` — structured data with `recommendation`, `summary`, `inlineComments`, `issueCounts` - `outputs/pr_review_general.md` — 1-2 paragraph general PR comment - `outputs/pr_review_comments/*.md` …

Senior Code Reviewer & Security Expert ## agent_task_preamble.md You are an agent triggered to perform a specific task. All required context — ticket description, PR diff, CI status, and related materials — has already been prepared in the `input/` folder. Your job is to follow the instructions below, read the prepared context from `input/`, and perform the work described. Do not ask for identifiers; the context is already available locally. ## review_coding_guidelines.md ```mermaid flowchart TD G1["⚠️ Review Guidelines — evaluate against existing codebase patterns"] G2["Before reviewing, explore the project's code structure, architecture, and testing patterns"] G3["If AGENTS.md exists → READ it — defines coding styles to check against"] G4["Flag deviations from established patterns unless justified in PR description"] G1 --> G2 --> G3 --> G4 ``` ## general_guidelines.md # PR Review General Guidelines ## Review flow ```mermaid flowchart TD START([PR ready for review]) --> READ["1. Read input context:
instruction.md, ticket.md, pr_info.md,
pr_diff.txt, pr_files.txt, ci_failures.md,
ci_failures_full.log, pr_discussions.md,
pr_discussions_raw.json"] READ --> DIFF["2. Run diff checklist on pr_diff.txt"] DIFF --> FILES["3. Read full content of every changed file"] FILES --> CODEGRAPH["4. Use CodeGraph:
callers/callees of changed symbols,
search for sensitive patterns,
impact analysis"] CODEGRAPH --> DIMS["5. Evaluate review dimensions:
Security · Architecture/OOP · Code quality
Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ### External-spec evidence rule A finding whose core claim is "**the spec / reference / ticket / external tool says or does X**" may be raised at 🚨 **BLOCKING** only when it quotes the exact source the review actually read during this run — a `file:line` reference or a doc URL. A bare "the spec says …" assertion is unfalsifiable for the author and for the machine, and a false one holds a validated PR hostage (live: a BLOCKING thread claiming an exemption list that the reference source did not contain — the reviewed code was behaviorally identical to it). Without a verifiable citation: - Downgrade the finding to ⚠️ **IMPORTANT**, phrased as a question: "Please confirm against `` — if confirmed, this becomes blocking." - Never let an uncited spec assertion be the sole reason for `REQUEST_CHANGES`. This is not a strictness cut: a spec-claim finding **with** a verifiable citation keeps full 🚨 BLOCKING force. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. Outputs Write the standard review artifacts: - `outputs/pr_review.json` — structured data with `recommendation`, `summary`, `inlineComments`, `issueCounts` - `outputs/pr_review_general.md` — 1-2 paragraph general PR comment - `outputs/pr_review_comments/*.md` …
Let me start by reading the input context to understand the task.

# Pull Request Information

- **PR #**: 1773
- **URL**: https://github.com/IstiN/flutter_agent_harness/pull/1773
- **Title**: refactor(1713): descend CRAP ratchets to 30.0 (app) / 12.0 (core) under crap4dart 0.14.2
- **Author**: vabhzw17eg2qu4m9-bit
- **Branch**: `refactor/1713-crap-descent` → `main`
- **State**: open
- **Files Changed**: 51
- **Additions**: +2790
- **Deletions**: -1585
- **Created**: 2026-10-21T21:18:06Z
- **Updated**: 2026-10-22T01:06:17Z

## PR Description

Closes #1713

Covers BOTH parts of the card: the flutter_app sandbox cluster (threshold restored 74.13 → 30.0) and the round-2 CORE ratchet (root threshold restored 90.0 → 12.0, the gh-1234 line). README CRAP badges synced back; `scripts/check_crap_guards.py` green (badge sync + exclude parity).

## Per-method CC (hand-computed, McCabe: base 1 + each if/for/while/case/`||`/`&&`/`??`/ternary)

CRAP = CC²·(1−cov)³ + CC (the 0.14.2 formula, verified against the card's measured table).

| Method | Before (CC @ cov → CRAP) | After (CC → est CRAP) | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `MemoryShell._runCommand` | 74 @ 97% → 74.13 | **3** → ~3.0 | Static `_commandRoutes` route table (`shell`, `ctx` closures), one entry per advertised command — aliases (`[`/`test`, `python`/`python3`, `xz`/`unxz`, `gzip`/`gunzip`, `pip`/`pip3`, `qjs`/`js`) and the `_hashCommands` family get their own entries; dispatch = guard-if + null-check + call. `_buildCommandRoutes` helper: CC 2. |
| `WasiSandboxShell._runBuiltin` | 43 @ 93% → 43.59 | **2** → ~2.0 | Same treatment: static `_builtinRoutes` table of `(s, st, o, src)` closures; every original per-builtin call signature preserved (that per-entry variance is why the table is data, not a switch); unknown-builtin fallback kept. |
| `detectLanguage` | 39 @ 100% → 39.0 | **3** → 3.0 | `_extensionLanguages` extension-map data table (37 keys, no dot, lowercased — byte-identical mapping incl. the `''`-ext and unknown-ext → `plaintext` paths). |
| `_connectionDisplayName` | 12 @ 42% → 40.58 | **5** → ~9.9 | Preset display-name switch extracted to `_presetDisplayNames` data table + `_presetDisplayName` (CC 2, `?? preset.name` fallback). Custom-row and `toString` arms unchanged. |
| `MemoryShell._interpretEchoEscapes` | 11 @ 43% → 33.58 | **3** → 3.0 | `_echoEscapes` data table + `_echoEscapeAt` seam (CC 3). Now covered by a new `echo -e` test (all five table arms + unknown-escape passthrough + trailing backslash) in `test/memory_shell_test.dart`. |
| `WasmSshCommands.builtinsFor` | 6 @ 0% → 42.0 | **6** → 6.0 @ 100% cov | CC already ≤ 30 once covered — the 0% cov was the whole CRAP story. New `test/wasm_shell_ssh_builtins_test.dart` drives all five local closures (read/write/kind/list/mkdir incl. parent-creation, sorted listing, missing → null) against a temp sandbox host dir; no SSH involved. |
| **core** `_typeName` | 9 @ 0% → 90.00 | **9** → 9.0 @ 100% cov | Pure name-table, CC already minimal — coverage was the problem. New `type naming in parse errors` group in `test/model_roles/providers_queue_test.dart` drives all seven arms (nothing/string/number int+double/boolean/object/array/runtimeType) through the public `parseProviderQueueEntries` error paths. |
| **core** `BindingProvenance.label` | 8 @ 25% → 35.00 | **1** → 1.0 | The switch duplicated the enum name arm for arm (all seven labels == `.name`). Getter is now `=> name` — CC 1, CRAP coverage-independent (≤ 2 at 0% cov). |

## Core-ratchet scoping note (round 2 addendum)

Both core offenders from the 2026-10-19 addendum are addressed in this PR — no scoping out: `_typeName` (90.00) and `BindingProvenance.label` (35.00) were the only core entries above the 12.0 line per the card's local reproduction on the merged core shards, so the root `crap4dart.yaml` threshold is restored 90.0 → 12.0 in the same commit train, with the badge synced and the `raise-issue: gh-1713` / Restored comment trail following the gh-992 precedent.

## Gates (run in the lane worktree on a standalone toolchain)

- `dart analyze` (standalone SDK) on `lib/src/model_roles` + `test/model_roles`: clean.
- `flutter analyze` on the four touched app lib files: zero findings from this diff (two `empty_catches` infos are pre-existing gh-925 guards, untouched; plus package-level flutter_inappwebview plugin-declaration noise).
- `dart test` `providers_queue_test.dart` + `provider_model_binding_test.dart`: **105 passed** (incl. the new type-naming group).
- `flutter test` on the touched app suites (memory_shell, wasm_shell pipeline/host-cwd/builtins/stat/ssh-builtins/modules, sandbox parity/job-log/conformance, provider_connection_guard): **473 passed** (incl. the new echo -e, display-name and ssh-builtin tests). Two compile bugs the analyzer gate alone did not surface (wildcarded closure params referenced in the body) were caught by exactly these runs and fixed before commit.
- `dart format` clean on every touched file.
- `flutter_app/lib/sandbox/wasm_shell.dart` stays under the 2800 loc gate: **2797**.
- `scripts/check_crap_guards.py`: ✅ (badge sync, exclude parity).

Note on CRAP numbers: the local agent cube cannot produce the lcov inputs (flutter coverage collector EPERMs through `.worktrees` — known, documented in `flutter_app/crap4dart.yaml`), so the after-CRAP column is computed from the formula at expected coverage, not locally re-measured. The CI app-crap-gate / core CRAP gates are the arbiter for both restored thresholds; suites above prove the behavior is unchanged so the coverage inputs should reproduce.

## Round 2 (CI validation): the four core offenders CI lcov surfaced

Run 39679365314 measured four functions above the restored 12.0 core line that the card's table did not list. All four descended on this branch (f9570fed31); threshold stays 12.0.

| Method | Before (CC @ cov → CRAP) | After (CC → est CRAP) | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `_cellRange` (timeline_projection.dart:314) | 14 @ 57.1% → 29.43 | **4** → 4.0 @ 100% | Start/duration lookups split into `_recordStart` (CC 7) + `_recordDurationMs` (CC 5); all arms covered by three new timed-mode tests (every anchored kind incl. compacted/system, unanchored/context drop, negative + missing duration clamps). |
| `AgentCliExt._extUpdatePlan` (agent_cli_ext.dart:398) | 7 @ ~26% → 26.50 | **7** → ~7-10 | Coverage fix: the local-path arm and the bare-source → local-installer arm now covered by two new `/ext update` tests (explicit local path re-plans → silent re-grant; a bare URL reports `update failed`, no network). `gh:`/`catalog:` arms stay uncovered — CRAP stays under 12 down to ~54% block coverage. |
| `_CatalogStreamFunction.call` (provider_catalog.dart:799) | ~9 @ ~40% → 26.13 | **4** → ≤ 7.5 worst case | The structural one: adapter dispatch is now a `_builders` route table (kind → builder); the four OpenAI-compatible kinds share one builder; the five family builders each keep CC 1, so their coverage no longer matters (≤ 2 CRAP each). Per-family options preserved byte-for-byte. |
| `_defaultRoleStyle` (tui_theme.dart:646) | 21 @ 100% → 21.00 | **1** → 1.0 | The 20-arm role-name switch is now the `_defaultRoleStyles` data-table lookup (identity values, `null` default via absent keys). |

Round-2 gates: `dart analyze` clean on the six touched files; `dart format` clean; `dart test` on timeline_projection / agent_cli_ext / provider_catalog_coverage / cache_routing / provider_identity suites: **58 passed** (incl. the 5 new tests). Shared-checkout hygiene: an initial mis-pathed edit batch landed in the shared checkout and was reverted to HEAD before reapplication (checkout verified clean, `git status` empty).


## Round 3 (CI recurrence on a6109ac8): the full 0.14.2 tier — 42 methods

Run 39692028722's core CRAP census (pulled from the job log) shows the card's round-2 table was only the tip: **42 methods measure > 12.0** under CI lcov — the fully-covered CC-13…21 dispatcher tier (which 0.14.2 counts higher than the CC-12 tier gh-1234 documented under 0.11) plus a 0%-cov CC-4 tier. All 42 descended in f9570fed31 + the follow-up commit; threshold stays 12.0, no re-raise.

| Method (file) | Before CC @ cov → CRAP | After CC → CRAP @ CI cov | Treatment |

+/// The normalized command handler signature of `MemoryShell`'s route
+/// table (`_commandRoutes`): one `(shell, ctx)` closure per advertised
+/// command (issue #1713, the #558 route-table pattern).
+typedef _CommandRoute =
+    Future<_StageResult> Function(MemoryShell shell, _Context ctx);
+
 /// A pure-Dart [Shell] that operates on a [MemoryFileSystem].
 ///
 /// This is the web fallback for the WASM-backed `WasiSandboxShell`: the
@@ -416,6 +422,99 @@ final class MemoryShell implements Shell, BackgroundShell {
     }
   }
 
+  /// Route table: command name → handler (issue #1713, the #558
+  /// route-table pattern). One entry per advertised command — aliases
+  /// (`[`/`test`, `python`/`python3`, `xz`/`unxz`, …) get their own
+  /// entries — and the checksum family is appended by
+  /// [_buildCommandRoutes]. Handlers normalize to `(shell, ctx)` so the
+  /// dispatch itself stays branch-free.
+  static final Map<String, _CommandRoute> _commandRoutes =
+      _buildCommandRoutes();
+
+  static Map<String, _CommandRoute> _buildCommandRoutes() {
+    final routes = <String, _CommandRoute>{
+      'true': (_, _) async => MemoryShell._ok,
+      'false': (_, _) async =>
+          const _StageResult(stdout: [], stderr: [], exitCode: 1),
+      'echo': (shell, ctx) async => shell._echo(ctx.args),
+      'cat': (shell, ctx) async => shell._cat(ctx),
+      'ls': (shell, ctx) async => shell._ls(ctx),
+      'mkdir': (shell, ctx) async => shell._mkdir(ctx),
+      'rmdir': (shell, ctx) async => shell._rmdir(ctx),
+      'touch': (shell, ctx) async => shell._touch(ctx),
+      'cp': (shell, ctx) async => shell._cp(ctx),

content.thinking:
The wire_protocol.dart change: encodeEvent switched from an exhaustive switch on sealed types to a `Map<Type, encoder>` lookup with `!` — `_eventEncoders[event.runtimeType]!(event)`.

Key behavioral difference: the original switch was EXHAUSTIVE over the sealed AgentEvent hierarchy — the compiler guaranteed all cases handled. The new map lookup uses `!` — if a new event type is added to the sealed hierarchy but not registered in the map, `encodeEvent` throws a null-check runtime error instead of a compile-time exhaustiveness error. This loses compile-time exhaustiveness safety — a real maintainability/correctness regression pattern. Same for `_kindOf`. That's worth an IMPORTANT finding (the map is typed `Map<Type, ... Function(AgentEvent)>` so any event type would be accepted, and a missing entry fails at runtime with an unhelpful null-check error, not at compile time).

Also note: `event.runtimeType` — if any event is a subclass of another event type (unlikely with sealed), keys mismatch. Fine.

All required context — ticket description, PR diff, CI status, and related materials — has already been prepared in the `input/` folder. Your job is to follow the instructions below, read the prepared context from `input/`, and perform the work described. Do not ask for identifiers; the context is already available locally. ## review_coding_guidelines.md ```mermaid flowchart TD G1["⚠️ Review Guidelines — evaluate against existing codebase patterns"] G2["Before reviewing, explore the project's code structure, architecture, and testing patterns"] G3["If AGENTS.md exists → READ it — defines coding styles to check against"] G4["Flag deviations from established patterns unless justified in PR description"] G1 --> G2 --> G3 --> G4 ``` ## general_guidelines.md # PR Review General Guidelines ## Review flow ```mermaid flowchart TD START([PR ready for review]) --> READ["1. Read input context:
instruction.md, ticket.md, pr_info.md,
pr_diff.txt, pr_files.txt, ci_failures.md,
ci_failures_full.log, pr_discussions.md,
pr_discussions_raw.json"] READ --> DIFF["2. Run diff checklist on pr_diff.txt"] DIFF --> FILES["3. Read full content of every changed file"] FILES --> CODEGRAPH["4. Use CodeGraph:
callers/callees of changed symbols,
search for sensitive patterns,
impact analysis"] CODEGRAPH --> DIMS["5. Evaluate review dimensions:
Security · Architecture/OOP · Code quality
Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ### External-spec evidence rule A finding whose core claim is "**the spec / reference / ticket / external tool says or does X**" may be raised at 🚨 **BLOCKING** only when it quotes the exact source the review actually read during this run — a `file:line` reference or a doc URL. A bare "the spec says …" assertion is unfalsifiable for the author and for the machine, and a false one holds a validated PR hostage (live: a BLOCKING thread claiming an exemption list that the reference source did not contain — the reviewed code was behaviorally identical to it). Without a verifiable citation: - Downgrade the finding to ⚠️ **IMPORTANT**, phrased as a question: "Please confirm against `` — if confirmed, this becomes blocking." - Never let an uncited spec assertion be the sole reason for `REQUEST_CHANGES`. This is not a strictness cut: a spec-claim finding **with** a verifiable citation keeps full 🚨 BLOCKING force. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. Outputs Write the standard review artifacts: - `outputs/pr_review.json` — structured data with `recommendation`, `summary`, `inlineComments`, `issueCounts` - `outputs/pr_review_general.md` — 1-2 paragraph general PR comment - `outputs/pr_review_comments/*.md` …
Let me start by reading the input context to understand the task.

{"path":"input"}

- **URL**: https://github.com/IstiN/flutter_agent_harness/pull/1773
- **Title**: refactor(1713): descend CRAP ratchets to 30.0 (app) / 12.0 (core) under crap4dart 0.14.2

- **Updated**: 2026-10-22T01:06:17Z

## PR Description

Closes #1713

Covers BOTH parts of the card: the flutter_app sandbox cluster (threshold restored 74.13 → 30.0) and the round-2 CORE ratchet (root threshold restored 90.0 → 12.0, the gh-1234 line). README CRAP badges synced back; `scripts/check_crap_guards.py` green (badge sync + exclude parity).

## Per-method CC (hand-computed, McCabe: base 1 + each if/for/while/case/`||`/`&&`/`??`/ternary)

CRAP = CC²·(1−cov)³ + CC (the 0.14.2 formula, verified against the card's measured table).

| Method | Before (CC @ cov → CRAP) | After (CC → est CRAP) | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `MemoryShell._runCommand` | 74 @ 97% → 74.13 | **3** → ~3.0 | Static `_commandRoutes` route table (`shell`, `ctx` closures), one entry per advertised command — aliases (`[`/`test`, `python`/`python3`, `xz`/`unxz`, `gzip`/`gunzip`, `pip`/`pip3`, `qjs`/`js`) and the `_hashCommands` family get their own entries; dispatch = guard-if + null-check + call. `_buildCommandRoutes` helper: CC 2. |
| `WasiSandboxShell._runBuiltin` | 43 @ 93% → 43.59 | **2** → ~2.0 | Same treatment: static `_builtinRoutes` table of `(s, st, o, src)` closures; every original per-builtin call signature preserved (that per-entry variance is why the table is data, not a switch); unknown-builtin fallback kept. |
| `detectLanguage` | 39 @ 100% → 39.0 | **3** → 3.0 | `_extensionLanguages` extension-map data table (37 keys, no dot, lowercased — byte-identical mapping incl. the `''`-ext and unknown-ext → `plaintext` paths). |
| `_connectionDisplayName` | 12 @ 42% → 40.58 | **5** → ~9.9 | Preset display-name switch extracted to `_presetDisplayNames` data table + `_presetDisplayName` (CC 2, `?? preset.name` fallback). Custom-row and `toString` arms unchanged. |
| `MemoryShell._interpretEchoEscapes` | 11 @ 43% → 33.58 | **3** → 3.0 | `_echoEscapes` data table + `_echoEscapeAt` seam (CC 3). Now covered by a new `echo -e` test (all five table arms + unknown-escape passthrough + trailing backslash) in `test/memory_shell_test.dart`. |
| `WasmSshCommands.builtinsFor` | 6 @ 0% → 42.0 | **6** → 6.0 @ 100% cov | CC already ≤ 30 once covered — the 0% cov was the whole CRAP story. New `test/wasm_shell_ssh_builtins_test.dart` drives all five local closures (read/write/kind/list/mkdir incl. parent-creation, sorted listing, missing → null) against a temp sandbox host dir; no SSH involved. |
| **core** `_typeName` | 9 @ 0% → 90.00 | **9** → 9.0 @ 100% cov | Pure name-table, CC already minimal — coverage was the problem. New `type naming in parse errors` group in `test/model_roles/providers_queue_test.dart` drives all seven arms (nothing/string/number int+double/boolean/object/array/runtimeType) through the public `parseProviderQueueEntries` error paths. |
| **core** `BindingProvenance.label` | 8 @ 25% → 35.00 | **1** → 1.0 | The switch duplicated the enum name arm for arm (all seven labels == `.name`). Getter is now `=> name` — CC 1, CRAP coverage-independent (≤ 2 at 0% cov). |

## Core-ratchet scoping note (round 2 addendum)

Both core offenders from the 2026-10-19 addendum are addressed in this PR — no scoping out: `_typeName` (90.00) and `BindingProvenance.label` (35.00) were the only core entries above the 12.0 line per the card's local reproduction on the merged core shards, so the root `crap4dart.yaml` threshold is restored 90.0 → 12.0 in the same commit train, with the badge synced and the `raise-issue: gh-1713` / Restored comment trail following the gh-992 precedent.

## Gates (run in the lane worktree on a standalone toolchain)

- `dart analyze` (standalone SDK) on `lib/src/model_roles` + `test/model_roles`: clean.
- `flutter analyze` on the four touched app lib files: zero findings from this diff (two `empty_catches` infos are pre-existing gh-925 guards, untouched; plus package-level flutter_inappwebview plugin-declaration noise).
- `dart test` `providers_queue_test.dart` + `provider_model_binding_test.dart`: **105 passed** (incl. the new type-naming group).
- `flutter test` on the touched app suites (memory_shell, wasm_shell pipeline/host-cwd/builtins/stat/ssh-builtins/modules, sandbox parity/job-log/conformance, provider_connection_guard): **473 passed** (incl. the new echo -e, display-name and ssh-builtin tests). Two compile bugs the analyzer gate alone did not surface (wildcarded closure params referenced in the body) were caught by exactly these runs and fixed before commit.
- `dart format` clean on every touched file.
- `flutter_app/lib/sandbox/wasm_shell.dart` stays under the 2800 loc gate: **2797**.
- `scripts/check_crap_guards.py`: ✅ (badge sync, exclude parity).

Note on CRAP numbers: the local agent cube cannot produce the lcov inputs (flutter coverage collector EPERMs through `.worktrees` — known, documented in `flutter_app/crap4dart.yaml`), so the after-CRAP column is computed from the formula at expected coverage, not locally re-measured. The CI app-crap-gate / core CRAP gates are the arbiter for both restored thresholds; suites above prove the behavior is unchanged so the coverage inputs should reproduce.

## Round 2 (CI validation): the four core offenders CI lcov surfaced

Run 39679365314 measured four functions above the restored 12.0 core line that the card's table did not list. All four descended on this branch (f9570fed31); threshold stays 12.0.

| Method | Before (CC @ cov → CRAP) | After (CC → est CRAP) | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `_cellRange` (timeline_projection.dart:314) | 14 @ 57.1% → 29.43 | **4** → 4.0 @ 100% | Start/duration lookups split into `_recordStart` (CC 7) + `_recordDurationMs` (CC 5); all arms covered by three new timed-mode tests (every anchored kind incl. compacted/system, unanchored/context drop, negative + missing duration clamps). |
| `AgentCliExt._extUpdatePlan` (agent_cli_ext.dart:398) | 7 @ ~26% → 26.50 | **7** → ~7-10 | Coverage fix: the local-path arm and the bare-source → local-installer arm now covered by two new `/ext update` tests (explicit local path re-plans → silent re-grant; a bare URL reports `update failed`, no network). `gh:`/`catalog:` arms stay uncovered — CRAP stays under 12 down to ~54% block coverage. |
| `_CatalogStreamFunction.call` (provider_catalog.dart:799) | ~9 @ ~40% → 26.13 | **4** → ≤ 7.5 worst case | The structural one: adapter dispatch is now a `_builders` route table (kind → builder); the four OpenAI-compatible kinds share one builder; the five family builders each keep CC 1, so their coverage no longer matters (≤ 2 CRAP each). Per-family options preserved byte-for-byte. |
| `_defaultRoleStyle` (tui_theme.dart:646) | 21 @ 100% → 21.00 | **1** → 1.0 | The 20-arm role-name switch is now the `_defaultRoleStyles` data-table lookup (identity values, `null` default via absent keys). |

Round-2 gates: `dart analyze` clean on the six touched files; `dart format` clean; `dart test` on timeline_projection / agent_cli_ext / provider_catalog_coverage / cache_routing / provider_identity suites: **58 passed** (incl. the 5 new tests). Shared-checkout hygiene: an initial mis-pathed edit batch landed in the shared checkout and was reverted to HEAD before reapplication (checkout verified clean, `git status` empty).


## Round 3 (CI recurrence on a6109ac8): the full 0.14.2 tier — 42 methods

Run 39692028722's core CRAP census (pulled from the job log) shows the card's round-2 table was only the tip: **42 methods measure > 12.0** under CI lcov — the fully-covered CC-13…21 dispatcher tier (which 0.14.2 counts higher than the CC-12 tier gh-1234 documented under 0.11) plus a 0%-cov CC-4 tier. All 42 descended in f9570fed31 + the follow-up commit; threshold stays 12.0, no re-raise.

Key behavioral difference: the original switch was EXHAUSTIVE over the sealed AgentEvent hierarchy — the compiler guaranteed all cases handled. The new map lookup uses `!` — if a new event type is added to the sealed hierarchy but not registered in the map, `encodeEvent` throws a null-check runtime error instead of a compile-time exhaustiveness error. This loses compile-time exhaustiveness safety — a real maintainability/correctness regression pattern. Same for `_kindOf`. That's worth an IMPORTANT finding (the map is typed `Map<Type, ... Function(AgentEvent)>` so any event type would be accepted, and a missing entry fails at runtime with an unhelpful null-check error, not at compile time).

Also note: `event.runtimeType` — if any event is a subclass of another event type (unlikely with sealed), keys mismatch. Fine.

wire_protocol.dart review:

1. **Loss of compile-time exhaustiveness**: `encodeEvent`, `encodeAssistantEvent`, `_kindOf` all became `map[runtimeType]!` lookups. New sealed-hierarchy event types now fail at RUNTIME (null check error) instead of compile time. The codebase values this safety (sealed classes used deliberately). This is a real maintainability regression — but is there a test that would catch it? A test could iterate over all AgentEvent subtypes... Actually there's a mitigation: `_eventDecoders` already existed as a table (mentioned "table-driven like [_eventDecoders]"), so this pattern pre-exists for decode. For encode, the old switch was exhaustive. IMPORTANT.

3. `runtimeType` keying: correct for sealed classes; but note the encoders do unchecked `event as XEvent` casts — a bug would put the wrong cast in the map. Type-safe enough.

Senior Code Reviewer & Security Expert ## agent_task_preamble.md You are an agent triggered to perform a specific task. All required context — ticket description, PR diff, CI status, and related materials — has already been prepared in the `input/` folder. Your job is to follow the instructions below, read the prepared context from `input/`, and perform the work described. Do not ask for identifiers; the context is already available locally. ## review_coding_guidelines.md ```mermaid flowchart TD G1["⚠️ Review Guidelines — evaluate against existing codebase patterns"] G2["Before reviewing, explore the project's code structure, architecture, and testing patterns"] G3["If AGENTS.md exists → READ it — defines coding styles to check against"] G4["Flag deviations from established patterns unless justified in PR description"] G1 --> G2 --> G3 --> G4 ``` ## general_guidelines.md # PR Review General Guidelines ## Review flow ```mermaid flowchart TD START([PR ready for review]) --> READ["1. Read input context:
instruction.md, ticket.md, pr_info.md,
pr_diff.txt, pr_files.txt, ci_failures.md,
ci_failures_full.log, pr_discussions.md,
pr_discussions_raw.json"] READ --> DIFF["2. Run diff checklist on pr_diff.txt"] DIFF --> FILES["3. Read full content of every changed file"] FILES --> CODEGRAPH["4. Use CodeGraph:
callers/callees of changed symbols,
search for sensitive patterns,
impact analysis"] CODEGRAPH --> DIMS["5. Evaluate review dimensions:
Security · Architecture/OOP · Code quality
Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ### External-spec evidence rule A finding whose core claim is "**the spec / reference / ticket / external tool says or does X**" may be raised at 🚨 **BLOCKING** only when it quotes the exact source the review actually read during this run — a `file:line` reference or a doc URL. A bare "the spec says …" assertion is unfalsifiable for the author and for the machine, and a false one holds a validated PR hostage (live: a BLOCKING thread claiming an exemption list that the reference source did not contain — the reviewed code was behaviorally identical to it). Without a verifiable citation: - Downgrade the finding to ⚠️ **IMPORTANT**, phrased as a question: "Please confirm against `` — if confirmed, this becomes blocking." - Never let an uncited spec assertion be the sole reason for `REQUEST_CHANGES`. This is not a strictness cut: a spec-claim finding **with** a verifiable citation keeps full 🚨 BLOCKING force. ## 7. Key behavioral difference: the original switch was EXHAUSTIVE over the sealed AgentEvent hierarchy — the compiler guaranteed all cases handled. This loses compile-time exhaustiveness safety — a real maintainability/correctness regression pattern. Same for `_kindOf`. That's worth an IMPORTANT finding (the map is typed `Map<Type, ... Function(AgentEvent)>` so any event type would be accepted, and a missing entry fails at runtime with an unhelpful null-check error, not at compile time).

Also note: `event.runtimeType` — if any event is a subclass of another event type (unlikely with sealed), keys mismatch. Fine.

1. **Loss of compile-time exhaustiveness**: `encodeEvent`, `encodeAssistantEvent`, `_kindOf` all became `map[runtimeType]!` lookups. New sealed-hierarchy event types now fail at RUNTIME (null check error) instead of compile time. The codebase values this safety (sealed classes used deliberately). This is a real maintainability regression — but is there a test that would catch it? A test could iterate over all AgentEvent subtypes... ## Per-method CC (hand-computed, McCabe: base 1 + each if/for/while/case/`||`/`&&`/`??`/ternary)

Key behavioral difference: the original switch was EXHAUSTIVE over the sealed AgentEvent hierarchy — the compiler guaranteed all cases handled. The new map lookup uses `!` — if a new event type is added to the sealed hierarchy but not registered in the map, `encodeEvent` throws a null-check runtime error instead of a compile-time exhaustiveness error. This loses compile-time exhaustiveness safety — a real maintainability/correctness regression pattern. Same for `_kindOf`. That's worth an IMPORTANT finding (the map is typed `Map<Type, ... Function(AgentEvent)>` so any event type would be accepted, and a missing entry fails at runtime with an unhelpful null-check error, not at compile time).

Also note: `event.runtimeType` — if any event is a subclass of another event type (unlikely with sealed), keys mismatch. Fine.

wire_protocol.dart review:

1. **Loss of compile-time exhaustiveness**: `encodeEvent`, `encodeAssistantEvent`, `_kindOf` all became `map[runtimeType]!` lookups. New sealed-hierarchy event types now fail at RUNTIME (null check error) instead of compile time. The codebase values this safety (sealed classes used deliberately). This is a real maintainability regression — but is there a test that would catch it? A test could iterate over all AgentEvent subtypes... Actually there's a mitigation: `_eventDecoders` already existed as a table (mentioned "table-driven like [_eventDecoders]"), so this pattern pre-exists for decode. For encode, the old switch was exhaustive. IMPORTANT.

2. `ModelRequestEvent` encoder keeps `'rawWireDump': ?e.rawWireDump` — raw wire dump can contain secrets; comment says redact via redactForLog before logging. Behavior unchanged (pre-existing), fine.

3. `runtimeType` keying: correct for sealed classes; but note the encoders do unchecked `event as XEvent` casts — a bug would put the wrong cast in the map. Type-safe enough.

## PR Description

Closes #1713

## Per-method CC (hand-computed, McCabe: base 1 + each if/for/while/case/`||`/`&&`/`??`/ternary)

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `MemoryShell._runCommand` | 74 @ 97% → 74.13 | **3** → ~3.0 | Static `_commandRoutes` route table (`shell`, `ctx` closures), one entry per advertised command — aliases (`[`/`test`, `python`/`python3`, `xz`/`unxz`, `gzip`/`gunzip`, `pip`/`pip3`, `qjs`/`js`) and the `_hashCommands` family get their own entries; dispatch = guard-if + null-check + call. `_buildCommandRoutes` helper: CC 2. |

| `detectLanguage` | 39 @ 100% → 39.0 | **3** → 3.0 | `_extensionLanguages` extension-map data table (37 keys, no dot, lowercased — byte-identical mapping incl. the `''`-ext and unknown-ext → `plaintext` paths). |
| `_connectionDisplayName` | 12 @ 42% → 40.58 | **5** → ~9.9 | Preset display-name switch extracted to `_presetDisplayNames` data table + `_presetDisplayName` (CC 2, `?? preset.name` fallback). Custom-row and `toString` arms unchanged. |
| `MemoryShell._interpretEchoEscapes` | 11 @ 43% → 33.58 | **3** → 3.0 | `_echoEscapes` data table + `_echoEscapeAt` seam (CC 3). Now covered by a new `echo -e` test (all five table arms + unknown-escape passthrough + trailing backslash) in `test/memory_shell_test.dart`. |
| `WasmSshCommands.builtinsFor` | 6 @ 0% → 42.0 | **6** → 6.0 @ 100% cov | CC already ≤ 30 once covered — the 0% cov was the whole CRAP story. New `test/wasm_shell_ssh_builtins_test.dart` drives all five local closures (read/write/kind/list/mkdir incl. parent-creation, sorted listing, missing → null) against a temp sandbox host dir; no SSH involved. |
| **core** `_typeName` | 9 @ 0% → 90.00 | **9** → 9.0 @ 100% cov | Pure name-table, CC already minimal — coverage was the problem. New `type naming in parse errors` group in `test/model_roles/providers_queue_test.dart` drives all seven arms (nothing/string/number int+double/boolean/object/array/runtimeType) through the public `parseProviderQueueEntries` error paths. |

## Core-ratchet scoping note (round 2 addendum)

Both core offenders from the 2026-10-19 addendum are addressed in this PR — no scoping out: `_typeName` (90.00) and `BindingProvenance.label` (35.00) were the only core entries above the 12.0 line per the card's local reproduction on the merged core shards, so the root `crap4dart.yaml` threshold is restored 90.0 → 12.0 in the same commit train, with the badge synced and the `raise-issue: gh-1713` / Restored comment trail following the gh-992 precedent.

## Gates (run in the lane worktree on a standalone toolchain)

- `dart analyze` (standalone SDK) on `lib/src/model_roles` + `test/model_roles`: clean.
- `flutter analyze` on the four touched app lib files: zero findings from this diff (two `empty_catches` infos are pre-existing gh-925 guards, untouched; plus package-level flutter_inappwebview plugin-declaration noise).
- `dart test` `providers_queue_test.dart` + `provider_model_binding_test.dart`: **105 passed** (incl. the new type-naming group).
- `flutter test` on the touched app suites (memory_shell, wasm_shell pipeline/host-cwd/builtins/stat/ssh-builtins/modules, sandbox parity/job-log/conformance, provider_connection_guard): **473 passed** (incl. the new echo -e, display-name and ssh-builtin tests). | `_CatalogStreamFunction.call` (provider_catalog.dart:799) | ~9 @ ~40% → 26.13 | **4** → ≤ 7.5 worst case | The structural one: adapter dispatch is now a `_builders` route table (kind → builder); the four OpenAI-compatible kinds share one builder; the five family builders each keep CC 1, so their coverage no longer matters (≤ 2 CRAP each). Per-family options preserved byte-for-byte. |
| `_defaultRoleStyle` (tui_theme.dart:646) | 21 @ 100% → 21.00 | **1** → 1.0 | The 20-arm role-name switch is now the `_defaultRoleStyles` data-table lookup (identity values, `null` default via absent keys). |

The wire_protocol.dart change: encodeEvent switched from an exhaustive switch on sealed types to a `Map<Type, encoder>` lookup with `!` — `_eventEncoders[event.runtimeType]!(event)`.

Key behavioral difference: the original switch was EXHAUSTIVE over the sealed AgentEvent hierarchy — the compiler guaranteed all cases handled. The new map lookup uses `!` — if a new event type is added to the sealed hierarchy but not registered in the map, `encodeEvent` throws a null-check runtime error instead of a compile-time exhaustiveness error. This loses compile-time exhaustiveness safety — a real maintainability/correctness regression pattern. Same for `_kindOf`. That's worth an IMPORTANT finding (the map is typed `Map<Type, ... Function(AgentEvent)>` so any event type would be accepted, and a missing entry fails at runtime with an unhelpful null-check error, not at compile time).

Also note: `event.runtimeType` — if any event is a subclass of another event type (unlikely with sealed), keys mismatch. Fine.

wire_protocol.dart review:

1. **Loss of compile-time exhaustiveness**: `encodeEvent`, `encodeAssistantEvent`, `_kindOf` all became `map[runtimeType]!` lookups. New sealed-hierarchy event types now fail at RUNTIME (null check error) instead of compile time. The codebase values this safety (sealed classes used deliberately). This is a real maintainability regression — but is there a test that would catch it? A test could iterate over all AgentEvent subtypes... Actually there's a mitigation: `_eventDecoders` already existed as a table (mentioned "table-driven like [_eventDecoders]"), so this pattern pre-exists for decode. For encode, the old switch was exhaustive. IMPORTANT.

2. `ModelRequestEvent` encoder keeps `'rawWireDump': ?e.rawWireDump` — raw wire dump can contain secrets; comment says redact via redactForLog before logging. Behavior unchanged (pre-existing), fine.

3. `runtimeType` keying: correct for sealed classes; but note the encoders do unchecked `event as XEvent` casts — a bug would put the wrong cast in the map. Type-safe enough.

Key behavioral difference: the original switch was EXHAUSTIVE over the sealed AgentEvent hierarchy — the compiler guaranteed all cases handled. The new map lookup uses `!` — if a new event type is added to the sealed hierarchy but not registered in the map, `encodeEvent` throws a null-check runtime error instead of a compile-time exhaustiveness error. This loses compile-time exhaustiveness safety — a real maintainability/correctness regression pattern. Same for `_kindOf`. That's worth an IMPORTANT finding (the map is typed `Map<Type, ... Function(AgentEvent)>` so any event type would be accepted, and a missing entry fails at runtime with an unhelpful null-check error, not at compile time).

Also note: `event.runtimeType` — if any event is a subclass of another event type (unlikely with sealed), keys mismatch. Fine.

1. **Loss of compile-time exhaustiveness**: `encodeEvent`, `encodeAssistantEvent`, `_kindOf` all became `map[runtimeType]!` lookups. New sealed-hierarchy event types now fail at RUNTIME (null check error) instead of compile time. The codebase values this safety (sealed classes used deliberately). This is a real maintainability regression — but is there a test that would catch it? A test could iterate over all AgentEvent subtypes... Actually there's a mitigation: `_eventDecoders` already existed as a table (mentioned "table-driven like [_eventDecoders]"), so this pattern pre-exists for decode. For encode, the old switch was exhaustive. IMPORTANT.

2. `ModelRequestEvent` encoder keeps `'rawWireDump': ?e.rawWireDump` — raw wire dump can contain secrets; comment says redact via redactForLog before logging. Behavior unchanged (pre-existing), fine.

3. `runtimeType` keying: correct for sealed classes; but note the encoders do unchecked `event as XEvent` casts — a bug would put the wrong cast in the map. Type-safe enough.

Key behavioral difference: the original switch was EXHAUSTIVE over the sealed AgentEvent hierarchy — the compiler guaranteed all cases handled. The new map lookup uses `!` — if a new event type is added to the sealed hierarchy but not registered in the map, `encodeEvent` throws a null-check runtime error instead of a compile-time exhaustiveness error. This loses compile-time exhaustiveness safety — a real maintainability/correctness regression pattern. Same for `_kindOf`. That's worth an IMPORTANT finding (the map is typed `Map<Type, ... Function(AgentEvent)>` so any event type would be accepted, and a missing entry fails at runtime with an unhelpful null-check error, not at compile time).

Also note: `event.runtimeType` — if any event is a subclass of another event type (unlikely with sealed), keys mismatch. Fine.

1. **Loss of compile-time exhaustiveness**: `encodeEvent`, `encodeAssistantEvent`, `_kindOf` all became `map[runtimeType]!` lookups. New sealed-hierarchy event types now fail at RUNTIME (null check error) instead of compile time. The codebase values this safety (sealed classes used deliberately). Actually there's a mitigation: `_eventDecoders` already existed as a table (mentioned "table-driven like [_eventDecoders]"), so this pattern pre-exists for decode. For encode, the old switch was exhaustive. IMPORTANT.

2. `ModelRequestEvent` encoder keeps `'rawWireDump': ?e.rawWireDump` — raw wire dump can contain secrets; comment says redact via redactForLog before logging. Behavior unchanged (pre-existing), fine.

3. `runtimeType` keying: correct for sealed classes; but note the encoders do unchecked `event as XEvent` casts — a bug would put the wrong cast in the map. Type-safe enough.

Key behavioral difference: the original switch was EXHAUSTIVE over the sealed AgentEvent hierarchy — the compiler guaranteed all cases handled. The new map lookup uses `!` — if a new event type is added to the sealed hierarchy but not registered in the map, `encodeEvent` throws a null-check runtime error instead of a compile-time exhaustiveness error. This loses compile-time exhaustiveness safety — a real maintainability/correctness regression pattern. Same for `_kindOf`. That's worth an IMPORTANT finding (the map is typed `Map<Type, ... Function(AgentEvent)>` so any event type would be accepted, and a missing entry fails at runtime with an unhelpful null-check error, not at compile time).

Also note: `event.runtimeType` — if any event is a subclass of another event type (unlikely with sealed), keys mismatch. Fine.

1. **Loss of compile-time exhaustiveness**: `encodeEvent`, `encodeAssistantEvent`, `_kindOf` all became `map[runtimeType]!` lookups. New sealed-hierarchy event types now fail at RUNTIME (null check error) instead of compile time. The codebase values this safety (sealed classes used deliberately). Actually there's a mitigation: `_eventDecoders` already existed as a table (mentioned "table-driven like [_eventDecoders]"), so this pattern pre-exists for decode. For encode, the old switch was exhaustive. IMPORTANT.

2. `ModelRequestEvent` encoder keeps `'rawWireDump': ?e.rawWireDump` — raw wire dump can contain secrets; comment says redact via redactForLog before logging. Behavior unchanged (pre-existing), fine.

3. `runtimeType` keying: correct for sealed classes; but note the encoders do unchecked `event as XEvent` casts — a bug would put the wrong cast in the map. Type-safe enough.

Key behavioral difference: the original switch was EXHAUSTIVE over the sealed AgentEvent hierarchy — the compiler guaranteed all cases handled. The new map lookup uses `!` — if a new event type is added to the sealed hierarchy but not registered in the map, `encodeEvent` throws a null-check runtime error instead of a compile-time exhaustiveness error. This loses compile-time exhaustiveness safety — a real maintainability/correctness regression pattern. Same for `_kindOf`. That's worth an IMPORTANT finding (the map is typed `Map<Type, ... Function(AgentEvent)>` so any event type would be accepted, and a missing entry fails at runtime with an unhelpful null-check error, not at compile time).

Also note: `event.runtimeType` — if any event is a subclass of another event type (unlikely with sealed), keys mismatch. Fine.

wire_protocol.dart review:

1. **Loss of compile-time exhaustiveness**: `encodeEvent`, `encodeAssistantEvent`, `_kindOf` all became `map[runtimeType]!` lookups. New sealed-hierarchy event types now fail at RUNTIME (null check error) instead of compile time. The codebase values this safety (sealed classes used deliberately). Actually there's a mitigation: `_eventDecoders` already existed as a table (mentioned "table-driven like [_eventDecoders]"), so this pattern pre-exists for decode. For encode, the old switch was exhaustive. IMPORTANT.

2. `ModelRequestEvent` encoder keeps `'rawWireDump': ?e.rawWireDump` — raw wire dump can contain secrets; comment says redact via redactForLog before logging. Behavior unchanged (pre-existing), fine.

3. `runtimeType` keying: correct for sealed classes; but note the encoders do unchecked `event as XEvent` casts — a bug would put the wrong cast in the map. Type-safe enough.

These are all faithful. In lsp_client, `_serverRequestResults` is `const <String, Object?>` — one subtle difference: previously `'window/showDocument'` responded `const {'success': false}` — new responds the same map from the table. Fine.

In lsp_tool, note the `_runLspOp` receives `arguments` and re-extracts line/character — the extraction was moved INSIDE `_runLspOp`. But there's a subtle detail: the original code extracted `line`/`character` BEFORE `cancelToken?.throwIfCancelled()` etc. — extraction order relative to nameError/other validations. Now line/character extraction happens later (inside _runLspOp). Purely local var extraction — no behavior change (they're just reads).

Key behavioral difference: the original switch was EXHAUSTIVE over the sealed AgentEvent hierarchy — the compiler guaranteed all cases handled. Also note: `event.runtimeType` — if any event is a subclass of another event type (unlikely with sealed), keys mismatch. Fine.

wire_protocol.dart review:

1. **Loss of compile-time exhaustiveness**: `encodeEvent`, `encodeAssistantEvent`, `_kindOf` all became `map[runtimeType]!` lookups. New sealed-hierarchy event types now fail at RUNTIME (null check error) instead of compile time. The codebase values this safety (sealed classes used deliberately). This is a real maintainability regression — but is there a test that would catch it? A test could iterate over all AgentEvent subtypes... Actually there's a mitigation: `_eventDecoders` already existed as a table (mentioned "table-driven like [_eventDecoders]"), so this pattern pre-exists for decode. For encode, the old switch was exhaustive. IMPORTANT.

2. `ModelRequestEvent` encoder keeps `'rawWireDump': ?e.rawWireDump` — raw wire dump can contain secrets; comment says redact via redactForLog before logging. Behavior unchanged (pre-existing), fine.

3. `runtimeType` keying: correct for sealed classes; but note the encoders do unchecked `event as XEvent` casts — a bug would put the wrong cast in the map. Type-safe enough.

Reviewing these:

1. **ain_auth.dart — `_stringOr` duplication**: `_stringOr` and `_intOr` are now defined in BOTH `ain_auth.dart` AND `copilot_device_flow.dart` (identical implementation). This is literally duplicated code introduced by the PR — the PR's own theme (round-3 table) says "shared `_stringOr`/`_intOr` default-helpers" per file, but the two files each define private copies. A shared util would better. That's a SUGESTION/IMPORTANT-level duplication finding (the PR's own diff-intro claims "shared _stringOr/_intOr over 4 token-field switches" — shared between call sites in that file, but duplicated ACROSS files).

Wait — original ain code: `refreshToken: switch (parsed['refresh_token']) { String value when value.isNotEmpty => value, _ => '', }` → new `refreshToken: _stringOr(parsed['refresh_token'], '')`. Faithful.

2. **silent_stream_policy.dart — `_isCommitEvent`**: The explicit 9-alternative true arm is replaced with `_ => true` relying on sealed exhaustiveness. Comment says classify new kinds explicitly. Behavior identical today. OK — this one actually keeps compile-time exhaustiveness? No — `_ => true` makes the switch non-exhaustive-checked (wildcard). If a new content-kind event is added to the sealed hierarchy, the default silently treats it as commit (true) — same as before? Before: new kind wouldn't compile (non-exhaustive switch). So this TOO trades compile-time exhaustiveness for runtime default. It's the deliberate PR pattern with a comment guard. Acceptable but worth noting once in the general exhaustiveness finding.

3. **transient_retry_stream.dart — `_resumeEvent`**: chained `??` over family helpers. Original: exhaustive switch. Order of checks: text family first, then thinking, then tool-call, then terminal. Same semantics since families are disjoint. Faithful. Note `_ => event` passes StartEvent through — same as before.

4. **rate_limit_info.dart**: `_rateLimitTitle` split — identical strings.

The wire_protocol.dart change: encodeEvent switched from an exhaustive switch on sealed types to a `Map<Type, encoder>` lookup with `!` — `_eventEncoders[event.runtimeType]!(event)`.

Key behavioral difference: the original switch was EXHAUSTIVE over the sealed AgentEvent hierarchy — the compiler guaranteed all cases handled. The new map lookup uses `!` — if a new event type is added to the sealed hierarchy but not registered in the map, `encodeEvent` throws a null-check runtime error instead of a compile-time exhaustiveness error. This loses compile-time exhaustiveness safety — a real maintainability/correctness regression pattern. Same for `_kindOf`. That's worth an IMPORTANT finding (the map is typed `Map<Type, ... Function(AgentEvent)>` so any event type would be accepted, and a missing entry fails at runtime with an unhelpful null-check error, not at compile time).

Also note: `event.runtimeType` — if any event is a subclass of another event type (unlikely with sealed), keys mismatch. Fine.

wire_protocol.dart review:

1. **Loss of compile-time exhaustiveness**: `encodeEvent`, `encodeAssistantEvent`, `_kindOf` all became `map[runtimeType]!` lookups. New sealed-hierarchy event types now fail at RUNTIME (null check error) instead of compile time. The codebase values this safety (sealed classes used deliberately). This is a real maintainability regression — but is there a test that would catch it? A test could iterate over all AgentEvent subtypes... Actually there's a mitigation: `_eventDecoders` already existed as a table (mentioned "table-driven like [_eventDecoders]"), so this pattern pre-exists for decode. For encode, the old switch was exhaustive. IMPORTANT.

2. `ModelRequestEvent` encoder keeps `'rawWireDump': ?e.rawWireDump` — raw wire dump can contain secrets; comment says redact via redactForLog before logging. Behavior unchanged (pre-existing), fine.

3. `runtimeType` keying: correct for sealed classes; but note the encoders do unchecked `event as XEvent` casts — a bug would put the wrong cast in the map. Type-safe enough.

The wire_protocol.dart change: encodeEvent switched from an exhaustive switch on sealed types to a `Map<Type, encoder>` lookup with `!` — `_eventEncoders[event.runtimeType]!(event)`.

Key behavioral difference: the original switch was EXHAUSTIVE over the sealed AgentEvent hierarchy — the compiler guaranteed all cases handled. The new map lookup uses `!` — if a new event type is added to the sealed hierarchy but not registered in the map, `encodeEvent` throws a null-check runtime error instead of a compile-time exhaustiveness error. This loses compile-time exhaustiveness safety — a real maintainability/correctness regression pattern. Same for `_kindOf`. That's worth an IMPORTANT finding (the map is typed `Map<Type, ... Function(AgentEvent)>` so any event type would be accepted, and a missing entry fails at runtime with an unhelpful null-check error, not at compile time).

Also note: `event.runtimeType` — if any event is a subclass of another event type (unlikely with sealed), keys mismatch. Fine.

wire_protocol.dart review:

1. **Loss of compile-time exhaustiveness**: `encodeEvent`, `encodeAssistantEvent`, `_kindOf` all became `map[runtimeType]!` lookups. New sealed-hierarchy event types now fail at RUNTIME (null check error) instead of compile time. The codebase values this safety (sealed classes used deliberately). This is a real maintainability regression — but is there a test that would catch it? A test could iterate over all AgentEvent subtypes... Actually there's a mitigation: `_eventDecoders` already existed as a table (mentioned "table-driven like [_eventDecoders]"), so this pattern pre-exists for decode. For encode, the old switch was exhaustive. IMPORTANT.

2. `ModelRequestEvent` encoder keeps `'rawWireDump': ?e.rawWireDump` — raw wire dump can contain secrets; comment says redact via redactForLog before logging. Behavior unchanged (pre-existing), fine.

3. `runtimeType` keying: correct for sealed classes; but note the encoders do unchecked `event as XEvent` casts — a bug would put the wrong cast in the map. Type-safe enough.

Key behavioral difference: the original switch was EXHAUSTIVE over the sealed AgentEvent hierarchy — the compiler guaranteed all cases handled. The new map lookup uses `!` — if a new event type is added to the sealed hierarchy but not registered in the map, `encodeEvent` throws a null-check runtime error instead of a compile-time exhaustiveness error. This loses compile-time exhaustiveness safety — a real maintainability/correctness regression pattern. Same for `_kindOf`. That's worth an IMPORTANT finding (the map is typed `Map<Type, ... Function(AgentEvent)>` so any event type would be accepted, and a missing entry fails at runtime with an unhelpful null-check error, not at compile time).

Also note: `event.runtimeType` — if any event is a subclass of another event type (unlikely with sealed), keys mismatch. Fine.

1. **Loss of compile-time exhaustiveness**: `encodeEvent`, `encodeAssistantEvent`, `_kindOf` all became `map[runtimeType]!` lookups. New sealed-hierarchy event types now fail at RUNTIME (null check error) instead of compile time. The codebase values this safety (sealed classes used deliberately). This is a real maintainability regression — but is there a test that would catch it? A test could iterate over all AgentEvent subtypes... Actually there's a mitigation: `_eventDecoders` already existed as a table (mentioned "table-driven like [_eventDecoders]"), so this pattern pre-exists for decode. For encode, the old switch was exhaustive. IMPORTANT.

2. `ModelRequestEvent` encoder keeps `'rawWireDump': ?e.rawWireDump` — raw wire dump can contain secrets; comment says redact via redactForLog before logging. Behavior unchanged (pre-existing), fine.

3. `runtimeType` keying: correct for sealed classes; but note the encoders do unchecked `event as XEvent` casts — a bug would put the wrong cast in the map. Type-safe enough.

Key behavioral difference: the original switch was EXHAUSTIVE over the sealed AgentEvent hierarchy — the compiler guaranteed all cases handled. The new map lookup uses `!` — if a new event type is added to the sealed hierarchy but not registered in the map, `encodeEvent` throws a null-check runtime error instead of a compile-time exhaustiveness error. This loses compile-time exhaustiveness safety — a real maintainability/correctness regression pattern. Same for `_kindOf`. That's worth an IMPORTANT finding (the map is typed `Map<Type, ... Function(AgentEvent)>` so any event type would be accepted, and a missing entry fails at runtime with an unhelpful null-check error, not at compile time).

Also note: `event.runtimeType` — if any event is a subclass of another event type (unlikely with sealed), keys mismatch. Fine.

wire_protocol.dart review:

1. **Loss of compile-time exhaustiveness**: `encodeEvent`, `encodeAssistantEvent`, `_kindOf` all became `map[runtimeType]!` lookups. New sealed-hierarchy event types now fail at RUNTIME (null check error) instead of compile time. The codebase values this safety (sealed classes used deliberately). This is a real maintainability regression — but is there a test that would catch it? A test could iterate over all AgentEvent subtypes... Actually there's a mitigation: `_eventDecoders` already existed as a table (mentioned "table-driven like [_eventDecoders]"), so this pattern pre-exists for decode. For encode, the old switch was exhaustive. IMPORTANT.

2. `ModelRequestEvent` encoder keeps `'rawWireDump': ?e.rawWireDump` — raw wire dump can contain secrets; comment says redact via redactForLog before logging. Behavior unchanged (pre-existing), fine.

3. `runtimeType` keying: correct for sealed classes; but note the encoders do unchecked `event as XEvent` casts — a bug would put the wrong cast in the map. Type-safe enough.

Key behavioral difference: the original switch was EXHAUSTIVE over the sealed AgentEvent hierarchy — the compiler guaranteed all cases handled. The new map lookup uses `!` — if a new event type is added to the sealed hierarchy but not registered in the map, `encodeEvent` throws a null-check runtime error instead of a compile-time exhaustiveness error. This loses compile-time exhaustiveness safety — a real maintainability/correctness regression pattern. Same for `_kindOf`. That's worth an IMPORTANT finding (the map is typed `Map<Type, ... Function(AgentEvent)>` so any event type would be accepted, and a missing entry fails at runtime with an unhelpful null-check error, not at compile time).

Also note: `event.runtimeType` — if any event is a subclass of another event type (unlikely with sealed), keys mismatch. Fine.
